questions.prompt: Which file descriptors are open by default in every process?
options: None: the program must open them
questions.explain: By convention 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, standard output and standard error. The shell sets them up before your program starts.

questions.prompt: A process closes descriptor 0 and then successfully calls `open` on a file. What does `open` return?
questions.explain: `open` (and `dup`) return the LOWEST unused descriptor of the process. After `close(0)` that is 0, so the file silently becomes the program's standard input.
option_notes: 3 is only the lowest free number if 0, 1 and 2 are open.

questions.prompt: `creat("log", 0640)` is equivalent to which call?
questions.explain: `creat` creates the file if needed, empties it if it exists, and opens it write-only.
option_notes: Opens read-only and does not truncate.
That opens read-write and appends instead of truncating.
Without O_CREAT the file is not created and the mode is ignored.

questions.prompt: What is true after `int fd2 = dup(fd1);`?
options: fd1 and fd2 share the same file offset
fd2 is the lowest unused descriptor number
Writing through fd2 changes the offset seen through fd1
questions.explain: Both descriptors refer to the same open file, so they share the offset and flags. They are closed independently, and the file stays open until both are closed.
option_notes: False: each descriptor is closed on its own.
True: dup picks the lowest free number.

questions.prompt: Opening the same file twice with `open` gives two descriptors with {{0}} file offsets (shared or independent?).
questions.explain: Each `open` creates a new open file description with its own offset. Only `dup`/`dup2` (and `fork`) share one.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of copying a file with system calls in order.
items: Open the source file with open(O_RDONLY)
Loop: read a chunk and write the bytes you got, until read returns 0
questions.explain: Always write exactly as many bytes as `read` returned (not the buffer size), stop when `read` returns 0 (end of file) and release both descriptors.

questions.prompt: Two descriptors are opened on the same file:
questions.explain: Each `open` creates its OWN entry in the system-wide table (with its own position) pointing to the same i-node, and the i-node counts 2 opens. Only `dup`/`dup2` share an entry (and raise its duplicates count).
options: The kernel creates 2 entries in the intermediate table (duplicates = 1 each) and the i-node's `nopens` is 2

questions.prompt: After `dup2(fd1, 1)`, how are the tables?
questions.explain: `dup2(old, new)` first closes `new` and then makes it refer to the SAME open-file entry as `old` (positions and flags are shared). No new open of the file happens, so `nopens` stays the same.
options: Descriptor 1 points to the same intermediate entry as fd1, whose duplicates count is now 2; the i-node's nopens does not change
A new entry is created and nopens grows
Descriptor 1 keeps its old file and fd1 points to the terminal
option_notes: No new entry: the entry is shared.
questions.code:
fd1 = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);   /* fd1 = 3, one entry (dup = 1), nopens = 1 */
dup2(fd1, 1);

questions.prompt: A process closes one of two descriptors created with `dup`. Can it still read through the other one?
questions.explain: `close` releases one descriptor. The underlying open file is released when the last descriptor that refers to it is closed.
options: Yes: the open file stays open until its last descriptor is closed
No: closing one closes the file for both
Only if it calls lseek first
option_notes: Each descriptor is closed on its own.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (The file contains abcdef; `dup` shares the position.)
questions.explain: `dup` makes both descriptors share ONE open file and one position: the first read consumes `a`, so the second returns `b`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (Same file, but two separate opens.)
questions.explain: Each `open` has its own position, so `fd2` still starts at the beginning and reads `a` again.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (lseek with SEEK_END.)
questions.explain: `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END)` returns the size (6). `lseek(fd, -2, SEEK_END)` goes to offset 4, which holds `e`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (O_APPEND always writes at the end.)
questions.explain: With `O_APPEND` the position is moved to the end before EVERY write, so the `lseek` to 0 has no effect on where the data goes.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (After the redirection the output goes to a file.)
questions.explain: `dup2(fd, 1)` makes descriptor 1 refer to the file: `after` is written to `o.txt`, not to the terminal. The `fflush` before it makes sure `before` was written to the terminal first.

questions.prompt: What does `read(fd, buf, n)` return at the end of the file?
questions.explain: `read` returns the number of bytes read; 0 means end of file and -1 means error (see `errno`). `EOF` is a stdio constant.
option_notes: That is only when n bytes were available.
System calls do not return EOF.

questions.prompt: What happens with `open("f", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL, 0644)` if `f` already exists?
questions.explain: `O_EXCL` together with `O_CREAT` means 'create it, but only if it does not exist yet'. It is used to avoid overwriting.
options: It opens and empties the file
It opens the file without changing it

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `open("f", O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC | O_CREAT, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR | S_IRGRP, S_IROTH)`?
questions.explain: `open` takes the permissions as one value: `S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR | S_IRGRP | S_IROTH`. Because `open` is variadic the extra argument compiles without error, and `S_IROTH` is lost. (A course slide example has this typo.)
options: The permissions must be ORed into ONE argument: the extra argument is silently ignored
O_TRUNC cannot be combined with O_CREAT
option_notes: The last argument is ignored, a real bug.

questions.prompt: Which statements about file descriptors are true?
questions.explain: A descriptor is a small non-negative number. A negative result (-1) means the call failed.
options: `open` returns the lowest descriptor number that is not in use
Each process has its own table of descriptors
A valid descriptor can be negative
0, 1 and 2 are standard input, output and error

questions.prompt: Complete the call so that the file is created if it does not exist and every write goes to the end.
questions.explain: `O_CREAT` creates the file when needed (and requires the permissions argument); `O_APPEND` appends.

questions.prompt: `write` returns the number of bytes actually {{0}}, which can be less than requested.
questions.explain: Always check the return value of `write`, and write exactly the bytes you got from `read`.

questions.prompt: Match each system call with what it does.
questions.explain: These are the basic file system calls of `<fcntl.h>` and `<unistd.h>`.
pairs: gets a descriptor for a file
copies bytes from a descriptor into memory
copies bytes from memory to a descriptor
changes the position in a file
makes one descriptor a copy of another

questions.prompt: Put the steps of redirecting standard output into a file in order.
questions.explain: Flush first (or the old text could end up in the file), duplicate onto descriptor 1, and close the extra descriptor.
items: Open the file with open(..., O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644)
Flush anything still buffered in stdout
dup2(fd, 1) so descriptor 1 refers to the file
Print: it now goes into the file

questions.prompt: Sort these calls into system calls and C library (stdio) functions.
questions.explain: System calls use integer descriptors and talk to the kernel directly; the stdio functions use buffered `FILE *` streams built on top of them.

questions.prompt: What is the type of the value returned by `read` and `write`, and why is it signed?
questions.explain: A signed type is needed to return -1 on failure. (Course slides write `size_t`, which cannot represent -1.)
options: `ssize_t`: it must be able to hold -1 for errors as well as byte counts

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (access tests a path.)
questions.explain: `access` returns 0 when the check succeeds and -1 when it fails. `F_OK` only tests that the file exists.
